Five stars all around for what it does - First of all, it's a fiddly filter so: Easy To Use: Meh, but AS GOOD AS COULD POSSIBLY BE EXPECTED; so five stars. Likewise, Easy To Clean rating.
We suspect the problems people are having with "blow-outs" of the mesh is not understanding what's at play:
There's a LOT of steam pressure (which can be great! Think steam engine, right!?) and it has to go somewhere. Not allowing the steam to pass through the filter will definitely cause blow-outs:
1) The ground should be a looser grind, like drip grind; more like what's in the pre-packs: NOT espresso grind which will pack tight and not allow the steam to a release.
2) Grounds should NOT be packed in: Again that steam needs to be able to flow THROUGH the grinds, not be BLOCKED by them.

Agitator manhandles clothing, will damage thin or delicate/worn clothing - I'm surprised nobody has mentioned this yet, though I have see a similar review for another model with a similar agitator - the big downside of this model and similar portable washers is that it really manhandles your clothes, meaning the agitator (thing on the bottom that spins) really grabs your clothes and thrusts them in the opposite direction with great force. This results in premature wear of your clothing. Thin T-shirts I had, had their necks stretched out. and delicate thin wool clothing had holes and tears created in them. Basically if you have any delicate or thin fabrics, they may get damaged, and even if they are not delicate, they will wear a lot faster or get stretched out more than if you washed it in a front load machine. I am not saying it is much worse than the other portable top load machines here with similar agitator designs. They all probably do the same thing.

Powerful Electric Cooktop - I ordered this simply for a couple of reasons: 1) Family likes cooking hot pot on special occasions and 2) Don’t want to use our gas stove since we have solar. There are some positives and negatives for this cooktop. I used it for a week now and found that it has certain limitations.
What I Observed:
1) The actual cooking area is 8.25 inches in diameter. It takes ANY kind of material for your pots/pans, unlike induction cooktops which won’t take certain material.
2) It heats up fast! I stir fried some veggies within 10 minutes. With that in mind, it gets hot fast. Would I buy this if I still had a toddler in the house? NO, unless I am constantly guarding it. The bottom and edge don’t get hot, but the center glows red (which could be too intriguing for little kiddos)
3) The cord is only 31 inches long. We had to use an extension cord for hot pot at the table.
4) There are 5 settings: Warm, Lo, Medium, Hi, and Sear. There’s a chart in the Instructions Manual of what each is capable of doing. I found that I only had to use the setting one below the recommended to get the job done.
5) One drawback of this electric cooktop is that it’s Maximum Run time is ONE HOUR. After which you have to let it cool down before using again. It hampers when using for hot pot or if everything you’re cooking takes longer than one hour. Hence, the 4 stars.
6) It is 120 V, 60 Hz, and 1200 W, pretty powerful. Maybe that’s why you can only use it for one hour at a time.
7) One year warranty

My conclusion is that it’s a good electric cooktop for fast cooking under an hour. Good as an extra burner. My son will inherit this when he goes to college. The price is very reasonable.

I use my 32-oz. mason jar to make the cold brew, and for that jar I put in two rounded to heaping tablespoons of FINE GRIND coffee (which I grind in my Blendtec blender -- by the quart) and fill with filtered water until about one inch or more from the top of the jar. (I discovered that filling the water too high does NOT work well with this filter.) I let it soak -- usually first for a few hours on the kitchen counter and then move to the fridge after that -- for average 12-plus hours.

I do not expect the jar not to leak, because I do not have a lid that can seal well over this. That works fine for me. I do not feel a need to shake up and down (though I do shake a little sideways).

Anyhow, I DO end up with a LITTLE bit of sediment, but not a bad amount at all and this is the best and easiest method I have found for brewing my coffee (which I tend to prefer cold). I only brew hot for friends or if I'm in a hurry.

Grounds always end up working their way inside the machine, and it takes tools to truly ensure it's all out. I'd been using the same machine since before Amazon was even around, but recently replaced it and decided to see what was new in accessories, too.

My new machine came with few extras, just a drip tray, couple different insert sizes for the handset, and a scoop/tamper. Before, I would've thought that's all you really needed. I was wrong.

When I first saw one of these filters, I knew I had to have one, and I was right. A carafe, espresso cups, a milk pitcher... all those things are nice, but unnecessary for making a superb latté. This filter not only keeps the machine far cleaner, but causes more evenly distributed waterflow throughout the grounds as well, ensuring a better brew, every time.

While I've always tried to ensure my grounds were evenly set before I tamp them, no amount of fuss with needles or other specialized tools made to separate coffee lovers from their money, can distribute those grounds in a way that totally prevents channels from forming. Those channels are visible evidence of uneven waterflow through the grounds, meaning not all grounds are getting the same flow. These filters are the only things I've seen that can fix that. They're not perfect, as they do have edges, but it's as vast an improvement over no-filter as espresso is over drip coffee (yes, that's my opinion - and I'm sticking to it!)

These filters should be as essential for making espresso as the handset, or at least the tamper. Such a serious improvement should always be incorporated into the basic process and included as essential equipment!

Love the pod, but the seal lids? Not as much. Overall, a good purchase. - So the nespresso pods have a flange that sticks out, ensuring you can only enter it into your machine in one direction, right? I bought one brand of refillable pod that includes that flange in the pop-off lid, and wouldn't you know--eventually the lid popped off and then I couldn't get the main body of the pod (which does not have a flange for the piston to push against) out of the piston. It took a lot of maneuvering but eventually I was able to get my thumb in the pod and press hard enough against the side of it to get some purchase and pull it out, but I have to say I was afraid I had ruined my machine for about 30 minutes. Luckily I was within the 30-day Amazon return window and was able to send the pod back. So next I decided to try this one since the flange is built into the body of the pod (yay!).

I have not been disappointed, although I have to say I think the stick-on seals are not necessary and I will not be buying them when I run out of the ones that came with the pair of pods. They seem to come unstuck sometimes (apparently when I overfill the pod), so, inspired by an instructable for reusing the aluminum Nespresso pods (which I don't think is a really good idea because they have holes poked in the bottom of them and are a soft aluminum), I make my own foil lids by cutting out 1-3/4" to 2" circles from chocolate bar foil (such as Green & Blacks, or Trader Joe's dark chocolate--regular kitchen foil would be too thick), and find it makes a better shot of espresso. You just have to make sure the silicone ring is not covered by the foil--use a fingernail to crimp it back into the groove near the edge after covering the top of the seal pod. Also make sure your chocolate bar foil is not too wrinkled because it may have holes in it that could affect the way pressure builds up inside the pod (you can hold it up to the light to make sure it doesn't have too many).
